title: Query Evaluation: Processing Models
short: One tuple, one batch, or the whole result?
lead: Compare how operators pass individual tuples, batches, or complete intermediate results to one another.
goals: Trace open, next, and close calls in the iterator model
Explain the state maintained by a selection, heap scan, and nested-loop join
Identify blocking operations such as sorting and hash-table construction
Explain pipelining, LIMIT, and iterator overhead

sections.title: Iterators give operators a shared interface
sections.html:
In the iterator model, operators share three operations: open() initializes their processing state, next() returns one tuple or EOF to signal the end of the input, and close() releases their resources. This common interface lets a parent operator request tuples from a child without needing to know whether that child is a heap scan or a complex join. Calls travel down from the root, and tuples are returned upward.

Original worked trace: Scan contains [2,7,4,9], Filter keeps x>5, and Project calculates x×10. On the first call to root.next(), Filter requests 2 and discards it, then requests 7 and returns it. Project returns 70. On the second call, Filter discards 4 and keeps 9, so Project returns 90. The third call returns EOF.

Key takeaway

One parent next() call may invoke the child’s next() method several times. A filter must keep requesting input until it finds a qualifying tuple or reaches EOF.

Related source material: PDF pages 2–6. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: State and blocking boundaries
sections.html:
A heap scan remembers its current page and slot. A nested-loop join remembers the current outer tuple and its position in the inner input. When the inner input is exhausted, the join restarts it and advances to the next outer tuple. A sort must inspect all of an unordered input before it knows the smallest item. An external sort may create runs during open() and merge them during next(). A hash join must finish building its hash table before it probes that table.

Pipelining passes results to the next operator as they become available, rather than writing and then rereading the whole intermediate result. It often reduces intermediate writes and the delay before the first output tuple. A blocking operator, such as a sort, still has to complete a preparatory phase before returning results.

Key takeaway

LIMIT 1 above a sort may still require reading the entire input. To determine the first row in global order, the sort must consider rows that have not yet been read. A left-deep plan shape does not remove this blocking requirement.

Related source material: PDF pages 7–13. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Vectorization and materialization
sections.html:
Original worked example: pass 100,000 tuples through 3 operators, with no operator reducing the tuple count. Tuple-at-a-time processing needs approximately 100,000×3=300,000 calls to pass tuples. With 1,000 tuples per batch, each operator processes only 100 batches, giving approximately 100×3=300 batch-passing calls. This count excludes EOF calls. If a filter is present, the number of later batches also depends on its output.

Batch processing spreads the cost of a call over many tuples, supports tight processing loops, and may use SIMD to process several values at once. Materialization instead retains an operator’s entire output before moving to the next step. This can improve locality by accessing nearby data in memory, but a large intermediate result puts pressure on RAM and I/O. Iterators, batches, and materialization are execution choices; each must preserve the result required by the query.

Related source material: PDF pages 14–18. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

Control flow, batches and complete intermediates

In a pull-based iterator or vectorized plan, the root requests work downward and tuples or batches return upward. A materialization model instead completes a child's intermediate result before the parent processes that result. This is an execution dependency, not an instruction that SQL operators change their logical meaning.

Tuple-at-a-time execution can suit a short request that consumes few rows; batches amortize calls and expose tight loops; materialization can exploit locality across a large intermediate. These are workload tendencies, not universal rankings. A filter changes downstream batch sizes, and blocking work remains blocking even when it uses batches.

Original boundary example: an input of 2,050 tuples with a maximum batch size of 1,000 produces batches of 1,000, 1,000 and 50 tuples, followed by EOF. The final partial batch is valid data; omitting it loses rows. The EOF marker is distinct from an empty qualifying result.

A batch size is 1,000 and 2,050 rows survive. What must the parent receive?

Worked answer. Three batches containing 1,000, 1,000 and 50 rows, then EOF. The result has all 2,050 rows.

Original explanatory extension supported by the cited core slides. Source PDF · physical pages 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18.

sections.title: Exercise: identify the pipeline segments
sections.html:
Consider Scan → Filter → Sort → Project → LIMIT 2. Which segments can stream their tuples to the next operator? Where can processing stop early and release resources?

Show the solution

Scan→Filter can stream. Sort blocks the first result until it has prepared enough data. After that, Sort→Project→LIMIT can stream. Once it has received 2 rows, LIMIT can stop requesting further tuples and call close() down the tree. Any temporary runs still need to be cleaned up. A top-k algorithm is an additional optimization outside this example; do not silently assume it is being used.

Related source material: PDF pages 9–13. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

quiz.question: Can one Filter.next() call invoke child.next() more than once?
options: Yes, to discard tuples that do not satisfy the predicate
No, it always calls the child exactly once
Only when the child is an index
quiz.explanation: The filter continues reading input until it finds a qualifying tuple or reaches EOF.

source.summary: The full official PDF has been reviewed. Coverage includes the open/next/close iterator interface and composability; selection, heap-scan, and nested-loop state; blocking sorts and hash builds; pipelining, LIMIT, and iterator overhead; vectorized batch and SIMD processing; and materialization, execution direction, and workload trade-offs. The explanations and calculations are original teaching material rather than reproductions of the slides.
